identity.title: Jumper Wires and Expansion Board
identity.subject_job_sentence: Jumper wires deliberately connect two different electrical points; an expansion board makes grouped connections easier to reach.

learning_objectives.statement: Name both endpoints of a planned jumper-wire connection before inserting it.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can write down endpoint A and endpoint B for a wire before I place it.

learning_objectives.statement: Explain that a wire's colour is a convention and not an electrical property.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can explain why two different-coloured wires can do the exact same job.

learning_objectives.statement: Make a labelled connection plan using the expansion board.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can trace the connection plan and complete the evidence card in order.

assumed_ideas: Five-hole groups share one clip; the centre trench does not.
prior_knowledge.retrieval_prompt: What did the last lab teach you about which holes share a connection?

misconceptions.misconception: A red wire always means power and a black wire always means ground.
misconceptions.why_it_is_common: Kits often ship wires in those colours by convention, so the colour looks like a rule.
misconceptions.confronted_by: The connection plan requires naming both real endpoints, which the colour alone never supplies.

vocabulary.child_definition: A single wire that connects exactly two chosen points.
One of the two named places a wire connects.

adult_does: Keep the board disconnected from any power source.
Verify the child's connection plan names both endpoints before any wire is inserted.
child_does: Name both endpoints of a planned connection.
Trace the connection plan on the map.
Tick each evidence-card item after checking it.
scaffolding.fading_note: The adult still confirms the safety state; the child now leads naming both endpoints before any wire touches the board.

cognitive_load.concrete_before_abstract: The child names two physical points before meeting the word endpoint.
cognitive_load.worked_example: The adult picks up one wire and says its two endpoint names aloud before miming where each would go.

engage.hook: The same wire could connect two completely different circuits depending only on where its two ends are placed.
engage.eliciting_question: Do you think a wire's colour changes what job it does?

predict.question: If you swap a red wire for a blue wire between the same two points, does the circuit change?
options: no, colour is just a label

observe.what_to_observe: First, that the two labelled ends joined by the dashed line on the map are the two ends of the one wire in your hand. Second, where the expansion row sits — the map shows it on its own, joined to nothing.
evidence_fields: the two named places this one wire would join
the expansion row I located, joined to neither end of the wire

steps.action: Check with the adult that no wire is connected to a power source.
Circle your prediction about wire colour.
Pick one wire and name its first planned endpoint.
Find one row on the expansion board the plan would use.
Trace the three locations on the connection plan with a finger.
Tick each place found and ask the adult to verify the card.

explore.expected_observation: The two ends of one wire are joined to each other, and the expansion row is a separate place joined to neither of them.

not_yet_outcome.symptom: The child names a colour instead of a location for an endpoint.
not_yet_outcome.first_check: Point to the physical hole or row again and ask for its location name, not its colour.

explain.what_you_saw: You saw that the two labelled ends on the map are the two ends of one wire, joined to each other. You found the expansion row on its own, joined to neither end.
explain.why_it_happened: A jumper wire is a passive conductor: it joins whatever two points it is plugged into, and nothing about its own colour changes that job. Wire colour is a convention some kits use to help people read their own plans, never an electrical property. An expansion board just brings grouped connections to a place that is easier to reach with a jumper.
explain.self_explanation_prompt: Tell the adult why naming a wire's two endpoints tells you more than naming its colour.

near_transfer: Plan a second wire's two endpoints using a different expansion board row.
far_transfer: A garden hose carries water between whatever two points it is connected to, regardless of its colour.
A phone charging cable works the same job whether it is white or black.

success_criteria_checklist: I can write down endpoint A and endpoint B for a wire before I place it.
I can explain why two different-coloured wires can do the exact same job.
I can trace the connection plan and complete the evidence card in order.

hinge_question.question: If a wire is coloured green but its two endpoints are on a rail and a resistor, what does the green colour prove about the circuit?
hinge_question.reveals: Whether the learner still treats colour as functionally meaningful instead of just a labelling convention.

evaluate.next_lab_link: L05 asks you to plan a resistor's two connection points the same way this lab planned a wire's.

identification.technical_name: male-to-male jumper wire and prototype-shield expansion row
identification.distinguishing_features: A flexible single-conductor wire with a rigid pin at each end. This unit also uses the kit's prototype shield, whose extra rows of holes are what 'expansion row' means here.
identification.orientation_cue: Do not infer a wire's job from its colour; an adult verifies the named endpoints against the connection plan.

parts.label: wire endpoint b
parts.role: The second point a jumper wire's connection plan names.

parts.label: expansion board row
parts.role: A grouped row of holes on the kit's prototype shield, reachable by a planned jumper.

troubleshooting.what_you_notice: You cannot remember which two points a wire was meant to connect.
troubleshooting.likely_reason: The connection plan was not written down before the wire was picked up.
troubleshooting.safe_first_check: Set the wire aside and re-write both endpoint names on the plan before touching the board.

troubleshooting.what_you_notice: Two wires of the same colour seem to be doing different jobs.
troubleshooting.likely_reason: Colour is only a labelling convention, so same-coloured wires can have completely different endpoints.
troubleshooting.safe_first_check: Check each wire's own endpoint plan instead of relying on its colour.

sourced_claims.claim: A conservative 1 A planning limit is used for 20 AWG breadboard jumper wire.

source_locator.section_or_line: these holes are sized to allow wire of up to 20 awg to be inserted

subject_scope.justification: The wire gauge a breadboard hole accepts is a property of the standard 0.1-inch board, not of one product.

sourced_claims.evidence_scope: The cited text establishes the 20 AWG gauge limit only. It states no jumper-wire current rating, so the 1 A figure is derived and marked as such rather than attributed to this source.

premises: The cited guide states a good-quality breadboard's contact current is generally limited to around 2 A.
A jumper wire's own contact is one of the two contacts in that path, so it cannot carry more than the path does.
1 A is chosen as half the cited 2 A path figure, as a deliberately conservative planning limit.
Nothing in this unit is energized, so no current flows and the limit is used for planning only.

sourced_claims.claim: The extra rows this unit calls an expansion row are the prototype shield's grouped holes.

source_locator.section_or_line: each of the rows of 5 holes has internal spring contacts that connect the 5 holes electrically

subject_scope.justification: What a grouped row of holes is electrically is standard breadboard construction, described generically by the cited guide.

sourced_claims.evidence_scope: The cited guide supports what a grouped row of holes does electrically, and nothing about which board ships in any particular kit. Which item in this kit carries those rows is scoped to the kit photograph and roster instead, and this claim no longer asserts that a separate 'breadboard expansion board' is in the kit.

quantities_taught.child_facing_meaning: A wire only joins the two exact points it is plugged into; naming both ends is how you know what it would connect.

behaviour.child_level: A wire is just a path between the two points you choose; it does not decide by itself what a circuit does.
behaviour.adult_level: A jumper wire is a passive conductor between two named endpoints; its colour is a labelling convention only, never an electrical property, and a connection plan must name both endpoints before insertion.
behaviour.simplification_check: The child account keeps the two-endpoint idea intact and omits wire-gauge and contact-resistance detail that does not change the safety-relevant fact being taught.

ratings_and_limits.parameter: conservative planning limit for breadboard jumper wire current, derived and not cited to a stated jumper rating
ratings_and_limits.source: Derived, not sourced. See content.sourced_claims: the cached guide states only that breadboard contacts take wire up to 20 AWG and that a good-quality breadboard is generally limited to around 2 A. No cited source states a jumper-wire rating.

failure_modes.wrong_action: Insert a wire without first naming both endpoints on the connection plan.
failure_modes.consequence: An unplanned connection could join two points that were never meant to be joined.
failure_modes.prevented_by: Write both endpoint names on the plan before any wire is inserted.
